title: a trust claim belongs to the resolved signature, so a marker on one overload does not certify the overload a call actually resolves to
notes: specification/compatibility.mdx, "Foreign Boundary": "Calling an unannotated foreign runtime value MUST add the checked `panic` case, because JavaScript and TypeScript may throw, reject, or violate a declaration." poc/src/language/README.md, `SMITHERS1502`: 'A trust claim belongs to the resolved signature, never to the symbol … Overload signatures are separate declarations of one symbol, so the old `symbol.declarations.flatMap(getJSDocTags).find(throws)` let one marked overload certify the unmarked, throwing overload a call actually resolved to.' Here the string overload is the dangerous one and is documented as throwing; the marker sits on the numeric overload. Nothing in the call's own text distinguishes it from a trusted call, which is what makes this the hardest half of the class to see by reading. DIRECTION, NOT LOCKED — and this case says so rather than claiming an obligation it does not have. docs/DECISIONS.md carries `@throws` overload resolution, multiple annotations and declaration merging as a **Direction** entry: "Exact rules for overloads, multiple annotations, declaration merging, validation, and generic error types remain to be specified", and conformance/COVERAGE.md 7.16 records that surface as unwritable for exactly that reason. What IS Locked is the default and its direction: compatibility.mdx §Foreign Boundary makes the panic case a MUST on every unannotated foreign call, and DECISIONS.md (Locked) makes `@throws {never}` "a trusted opt-out from the default `panic` case" — one claim, about one call. A claim the compiler cannot reduce to a single usable answer for the call in front of it therefore does not opt out, and the MUST stands. This case pins that fail-closed reading and the implementations' chosen behaviour, which BOTH BACKENDS AGREE ON; it does not settle the Direction entry. If the specification later chooses a different rule, THIS CASE IS REWRITTEN — it is not evidence against the new sentence.
